To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

perceived ingroup effectiveness (vs. ineffectiveness) generates stronger ingroup identification, which is mediated by emotional climate, ingroups anomie, trust in the group’s control system, and emotions.
perceived ingroup effectiveness in controlling its deviant members increases identification with the group.
perceived ingroup social effectiveness increases ingroup identification, and perceived ingroup social ineffectiveness decreases ingroup identification.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of perceived social control in ingroup identification, and the mediating processes involved.
the role of perceived social control on ingroup identification, and it provides a novel approach to understanding the relationship between perceived social control and ingroup identification.
the role of perceived social control on group identification and emotional climate, and the role of emotional climate and perceived social control in predicting group identification.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
social control is a key factor in the formation of group identification, as well as in the maintenance of group identity.

perceived group effectiveness is a strong predictor of ingroup identification and that this relationship is mediated by emotional climate, confidence in the social control system, anomie, and emotions.
the results of the present study support the hypothesis that perceived ingroup effectiveness in dealing with deviance increases ingroup identification.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effectiveness of a group’s social control is a critical determinant of ingroup identification.
the effectiveness of the ingroup’s ability to effectively deal with deviant members is a crucial element for the maintenance of the ingroup and the development of ingroup identification.
perceived ingroup effectiveness (vs. ineffectiveness) is positively (vs. negatively) associated with ingroup identification, and this effect is mediated by emotional climate (Study 3).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ability of a group to control deviant members can have a significant impact on the group’s social identity.
perceived social control can be a powerful predictor of ingroup identification.
ingroup identification is a function of perceived group effectiveness in dealing with deviant members, via the group’s social-control system.
